technique: verbs over adjectives — how the action words carry the weight
lesson:
Today we work on verbs. A verb is an action word. It tells you what someone or something does.

This poem leans on verbs instead of describing words. Look at "worn smooth on the one side." The verb "worn" does the work. You picture years of hands on that latch without being told the latch is old. Look at "the frost has stiffened the grass." "Stiffened" shows you the cold doing something. And "how one good turn done quiet can warm all the way." "Warm" is the whole point of the line.

It works because an action word makes you see motion. Your mind follows the doing. A describing word just sits there, but a verb pulls you forward to what happens next.

Try this: find one describing word in your draft and swap it for a verb that does the same job.

The second time through, count the verbs and hear how often they carry the line. Here is the poem.
poem:
The gate latch sits cold where your hand will find it,
same bar, same iron, worn smooth on the one side
from all the mornings you've lifted it half-asleep.
Outside the frost has stiffened the grass to gray wire
and the long dry of this fall has the ground asking
for rain that keeps hanging back, careful, unsure.
You know a little about holding things steady—
how a day gets set in motion while you're still dreaming,
how one good turn done quiet can warm all the way
into someone else's evening, and come back changed.
The kettle's on. The latch is waiting for your thumb.
You carried something out into the dark last night—

The soup went warm in someone's hands last night—
go be that kind of good again.
